articles.title: Croatian court approves extradition in Nord Stream bombing case
articles.summary: Nord Stream sabotage suspect to be extradited from Croatia; court ruling faces appeal with final decision still pending.
articles.body:
A Croatian court has approved the extradition of a Ukrainian man wanted in Germany in connection with the 2022 undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines.

The man was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August while reportedly working on a Hollywood dramatisation of the attack, according to the AFP news agency.

On Thursday, his lawyer, Ljubo Pavasovic Viskovic, said the court approved the extradition on September 18.

Pavasovic Viskovic added that the ruling is not final and will be appealed, so it is unclear when or whether the extradition will take place.

German prosecutors identified the man as Vladimir Z.

They said the suspect was a “trained scuba diver” who was part of a team that allegedly “planted explosives” on the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of Bornholm.

The undersea blasts on September 26, 2022, damaged the pipelines, which had been built to carry natural gas from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea.

In July, German federal prosecutors filed charges against a former Ukrainian army officer in connection with the explosions.

Prosecutors accuse Vladimir Z of working closely with another Ukrainian identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K . He was detained in August 2025 during a raid on the bungalow in an Italian village where he was staying with his family. He was then extradited to Germany in November last year.

Serhii K is due to face trial at the Hamburg Higher Regional Court on October 14, and the proceedings could continue through February 2027.

The Nord Stream attacks came months after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, destroying three of the four pipelines of the major energy link at a time when European countries were trying to gradually wean themselves off Russian energy.

German investigators believe a Ukrainian state agency ordered the attack to deprive Russia of revenues to finance its invasion of Ukraine.

The case is politically awkward for Germany and Ukraine, as Berlin has been one of Kyiv’s strongest supporters in its fight against Russia.

German government officials, when asked about the issue, have pointed to the judiciary’s independence.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said his government knew nothing about any plan to blow up the pipelines.

articles.title: Blood test call for people potentially impacted by cancer-causing chemicals in the ground
articles.summary: People living near a lagoon branded "a shame on Britain" want to be tested for cancer-causing PCBs.
articles.body:
When she moved to the countryside two years ago, Natalie Dugdale thought it would be the perfect spot to raise her family.

Close to a lagoon in north Wales, she thought she could walk her baby, toddler and dogs on public footpaths.

But when she watched Michael Sheen's BBC documentary revealing the lagoon's history as a dumping ground of cancer-causing chemicals known as PCBs, Natalie was shocked.

Now she is part of a group of people who are worried they may have been poisoned by years of exposure to toxic waste, and are campaigning for voluntary blood testing across Wales.

But Wales' public health body has said it does not recommend blood testing for PCBs, saying it would cause more concern.

Public Health Wales (PHW) said the tests did not provide "a reliable means of assessing an individual's exposure to contamination or the potential health impact".

Members of a newly formed campaign group for those living alongside some of the sites concerned have told BBC Wales they had been left "frightened and upset" and said testing would help provide "peace of mind".

Natalie could not believe her local lake in Llwyneinion, just outside Wrexham, had actually once been a dumping ground for potentially dangerous chemicals and wants to see blood testing introduced.

"I was really upset because having young children, what are they being exposed to?," said Natalie, 33.

Llwyneinion lagoon was recently branded "a shame on Britain", following the documentary into historical dumping of PCBs by US chemical giant Monsanto, which had factories in Wrexham and Newport.

Michael Phillips played at the lagoon as a child and decades later developed a rare cancer in his shoulder. He said many of his other friends had died because of similarly rare cancers, which he now suspects were linked, although no proven link has been established.

"I would say every person that played in the pool that was close to me, apart from one friend who had an operation to get rid of it, is dead," said Michael, 63.

Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country.

Michael Phillips was also found to have "very high" levels of PCBs in his blood, after private testing commissioned for the documentary.

The banned chemicals were once widely used and revered for being non-flammable and hard to break down – but are seen today as the first "forever chemicals" - which are building up in the environment, threatening wildlife and human health.

Michael and Natalie have both now joined a newly formed campaign group - made up of hundreds of residents living alongside the former Monsanto works in the villages of Cefn Mawr, Acrefair and Trevor in north-east Wales.

One of their calls - alongside a national soil testing programme - is for voluntary blood testing, led by Public Health Wales.

One of the group's founders pointed to the fact the documentary had to rely on a large-scale study from the US to assess and compare PCB levels in the local residents it had tested.

"There's a huge potential here for Wales... to really lead the way and show the rest of the UK how to handle this risk," said community councillor Katie Witherden.

"It would give people answers about what they have or haven't been exposed to - and I think all of us deserve the right to have the choice to know that."

Nel Byers said that blood testing was needed "for people's own peace of mind" as well as showing "on a national scale" whether these communities had heightened results.

"If they get the blood testing done they might actually start doing something about [the dumpsites]," said the 33-year-old from Trevor.

Public Health Wales issued a statement in response to calls from residents and politicians - including the Welsh Affairs Select Committee of MPs - saying a programme of blood testing was "not recommended".

It argued that testing would "not tell us how or where people may have been exposed" as there were many potential PCB sources in the wider environment - including food, and materials in homes and buildings.

There was no treatment for higher levels of the chemicals so there was a risk too of "causing worry among people who are found to have PCBs in their blood", it added.

Natalie said she found the response "disappointing", adding: "I think a lot of people are already frightened and it's more frightening not knowing."

Katie agreed that "people are already worried" and said: "We know they can't treat PCBs and that's not what we're asking for."

Her husband Steve Witherden is the Labour MP for Montgomeryshire and Glyndŵr and described PHW's response as "chilling".

"My hope is that they revise their position," he said.

"There's a real strength of feeling from people who've lived near to these sites or worked in them, a real clamouring."

The debate comes after privately funded testing found high levels of other so-called forever chemicals in dozens of people living near a chemical factory in Lancashire.

Dr Dave Megson, of Manchester Metropolitan University, who was also involved in the Buried documentary testing, argued the US and other countries in Europe were well ahead of the UK in advancing the use of blood testing for alleged chemical contamination.

While it could not prove that cancers and other health impacts were caused by PCBs, he argued: "There's so much information that we can pull out if you use those non-standard tests and do some advanced science."

Public Health Wales has acknowledged the health authority's refusal to back calls for blood testing was "a difficult message".

"We appreciate that the communities are worried and that is understandable, but the testing isn't necessarily going to give any good answers," said Prof Sarah Jones, consultant in environmental public health at PHW.

"Generally when we do any sort of testing we want to be able to put things right for people and that's what we can't do here."

She argued that there were too many "unknowns" about the impacts of concentrations of PCBs on the body and no treatment for those found to have elevated levels in their blood.

"All we could do is give [people] a number that we can't really interpret and then we can't make right."

She felt this could "create even more worry and that is a health harm in itself."

"There is nothing that blood testing can do that would magically take those worries away - it would only potentially magnify them," Jones said.

Asked whether the cost of implementing a blood testing regime was also a factor, she said: "No... this is not about money."

Rather than blood testing, Jones argued public authorities should focus on taking "whatever steps need to be taken to make these [suspected dumpsites] as safe as possible".

Dr Will Mackintosh, from the Royal College of GPs Cymru, said it may be that "additional support" will be required for GPs in communities where concerns have been raised about alleged contamination in future.

"It's clearly something which obviously large numbers of people are concerned about, and general practice has a role in responding to that as best as we can," he said.

The Welsh government has said that "addressing the issue of contaminated land is a key priority for this government".

"We will develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks," the government said.

"This will include strengthening the 'polluter pays principle' while we continue to press for environmental justice by raising the importance of seeking UK Government funding direct with the UK Treasury.

"This should be used to continue our joint efforts to address the legacy of Wales' industrial past through restoring coal tips and remediation of contaminated land."

Monsanto does not exist any more and Eastman Chemical Company, responsible for the firm's legacy production in the UK, has not responded to BBC Wales' requests for comment.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Meeting on the margins of United Nations General Assembly, G4 countries called for a reform of the UNSC at the earliest, saying in a joint statement that the council is currently unable to effectively discharge its core responsibility of maintaining international peace and security.The G4 group of countries (India, Japan, Brazil, and Germany) supports urgent reforms of the security council through the expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories of membership of UNSC."Discussed the imperative of reformed multilateralism and a more representative, responsive and effective UN Security Council that reflects today's global realities. articles.title: A Frank Lloyd Wright house in Michigan fell into disrepair before a couple bought and restored it in 2016; the 2,500-sq-ft home on 2 acres now earns about $180,000-$200,000 a year and is listed for $2.1 million
articles.summary: Tucked into a landscape of mature trees, rolling hills and open meadows in Galesburg, Michigan, a Frank Lloyd Wright house seems to disappear into its
articles.body: Tucked into a landscape of mature trees, rolling hills and open meadows in Galesburg, Michigan, a Frank Lloyd Wright house seems to disappear into its surroundings rather than sit apart from them. Built more than seven decades ago, the 2,500-square-foot home is now back in the spotlight after a careful restoration, and it comes with an unusual income stream. The Samuel Eppstein House, listed for $2.1 million, is one of just four Wright-designed homes in The Acres, a 70-acre community conceived by the celebrated architect as an intimate experiment in Usonian living, states Realtor's online report.A rare Wright communityThe Acres is considered the only community composed entirely of Frank Lloyd Wright houses. Wright originally envisioned a larger collection of homes, but only four were ultimately built. The Eppstein House was completed in 1953 for Samuel and Dorothy Eppstein, scientists at pharmaceutical company Upjohn. The couple worked closely with Wright and even made modifications to aspects of his original design. They also cast some of the concrete blocks used in the house themselves, adds the report. Concrete-block construction, extensive windows and a close relationship with the landscape are hallmarks of the home. Rather than separating the interiors from the outdoors, the design continually draws the surrounding landscape into view.Restored without losing its characterThe house eventually fell into disrepair before Marika Broere and Tony Hillebrandt purchased it in 2016. The couple undertook a restoration that brought the property back into usable condition while retaining its original architectural character. Modern additions included air conditioning, while some interior spaces were reworked for contemporary living. Two bedrooms were combined into one larger primary bedroom, and the main bathroom received an updated, more spacious shower. The result is a three-bedroom, two-bathroom home that retains its mid-century character. Wood surfaces, expansive windows and distinctive red concrete floors remain central to the interiors, with much of the existing furniture included in the sale.Two acres inside a 70-acre landscapeThe property occupies two acres within The Acres' larger shared landscape. Mature trees, meadows and gently rolling terrain surround the four Wright homes, creating a setting where the architecture and natural environment are closely intertwined, adds the Realtor report.The home's layout reinforces that connection. Windows are positioned throughout the living areas, offering changing views of the landscape and allowing daylight to shape the interiors. For buyers interested in architectural history, the setting is as significant as the structure itself. The property offers the chance to live inside one of Wright's planned communities while remaining immersed in the landscape that shaped its design, informs the report.A home that doubles as a businessBeyond its architectural appeal, the Eppstein House has also become a substantial short-term rental. Its current owners have spent roughly half the year using the property themselves and rented it during the remainder. That arrangement has generated approximately $180,000 to $200,000 in annual income. Guests have traveled from across the United States and internationally to stay at the property, while the house has also been used for corporate retreats and photo shoots.Now listed for $2.1 million, the Eppstein House offers a rare combination of a restored piece of Frank Lloyd Wright history, two acres of Michigan landscape and an established rental business, all wrapped into one unusually distinctive property.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and RealtorReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: The best tablets for every budget, whether you stream, take notes or work on the go
articles.summary: From Apple’s latest iPads to affordable Android and Amazon Fire tablets, here’s how to choose the best tablet for streaming, work, reading and more.
articles.body: Laptops offer plenty of power, but they’re not always the easiest thing to carry around. Tablets, on the other hand, tend to be more portable, less bulky and now, often mirror the functions of a full-size computer. NBC Selected editors have used tablets as computer replacements and entertainment centers for years, and one thing keeps them coming back: the weight. At around a pound, tablets are simple to travel with and tuck into a bag or store away when you don’t need them. Once you add a keyboard or stylus, they’re good for taking notes, building presentations and more. If you’re thinking about getting one for yourself check out our below list of NBC Selected editor-approved tablets, along with expert advice on how to find the right one for you. The best tablets of 2026 The tablet picks below come highly recommended by NBC Selected editors or are in line with guidance from our expert Alan Elterman, a sales manager at Abt, a national retailer of electronics and appliances, and what he said you should prioritize when shopping. Apple’s most affordable iPad is perfect for making video calls, watching shows and reading books. It has a large screen and speakers on each side for stereo-like audio. “I typically use a tablet as my entertainment device when a laptop would be too cumbersome — it’s a great travel tool for that reason,” says former NBC Selected tech reporter Harry Rabinowitz. “As such, I need my tablet to do a handful of things: browse the web, watch videos, join video calls and send the occasional email.” This iPad is powered by Apple’s A16 chip, which keeps everyday tasks like streaming, browsing and video calls running smoothly, and its 11-inch Liquid Retina display makes shows and photos look crisp and vibrant. The 12MP front camera automatically keeps you centered in frame during video calls — a small but handy touch for anyone who moves around while chatting. With Wi-Fi 6 for fast, reliable connections and up to 10 hours of battery life, it’s built to keep up whether you’re working from a coffee shop or unwinding on a long flight. The iPad mini has an 8.3-inch screen, but don’t let the size fool you — it still delivers a full 10 hours of battery life, and an anti-reflective coating actually gives it better color contrast than the base iPad (A16). The compact frame means it’s easier to hold with one for long stretches and slips easily into a bag or backpack without adding bulk. I own one myself — I originally bought it for my daughter to use on a cross-country flight, but I’ve since claimed it as my own because I love how compact it is. It’s become my go-to travel companion, and at night I use it in bed to catch up on my favorite reality television shows or to read on the Kindle app before falling asleep. NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin bought an iPad Pro, plus the Apple Magic keyboard case and Apple Pencil, when she was in college. She was looking for a lightweight device that could replace her laptop — lugging it around campus weighed down her backpack. The iPad Pro (plus accessories) was a big investment, but says it was one of the best she made during school. “I used it to type essays, read e-books, highlight digital textbooks, draw for the school newspaper — I used it for everything,” says Malin. Nowadays, she mostly uses it for workout apps at home. The screen is big and bright, and the speakers get so loud that she never finds herself setting it higher than 50 percent volume, even while exercising. Malin bought an older generation of this iPad Pro, but the current model, now powered by Apple’s M5 chip, is significantly faster, especially for AI-driven tasks, according to the brand. It also keeps the OLED display and ultra-thin design for a sleek and effective tablet and smart laptop replacement choice for those looking. The Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE is a mid-range tablet built for Android users. It has a 10.9-inch IPS LCD display and an S Pen comes included at no extra cost, making it a natural fit for note taking, sketching, and annotating documents. It also carries an IP68 water and dust resistance rating along with a sizable 8,000mAh battery that can last up to 20 hours on a single charge. Beyond the core specs, the Tab S10 FE holds up well for everyday use. Its 13MP rear camera and 12MP front camera cover the basics for video calls and document scanning, while dual speakers and expandable storage via microSD (up to 2TB) round out its practical appeal. The latest Surface Pro has a vibrant OLED PixelSense touchscreen that is great for editing photos, streaming video, or taking notes with a stylus. It’s powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite 12-core processor, a jump from previous Surface Pro chips that brings faster, AI-accelerated performance for multitasking and heavy workloads, along with built-in Copilot AI assistance through Windows 11. This configuration comes with 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage, giving you solid room for everyday productivity and creative work. It also has a built-in kickstand that adjusts up to 165 degrees, letting it function as a laptop, a tablet, an e-reader reader and more, and Microsoft rates the battery for up to 15.5 hours of local video playback. Two USB-C/USB4 ports handle charging, fast data transfer, and external display connections. It’s worth noting that the keyboard and Surface Pen are sold separately, so factor those into your budget if you want the full laptop-like experience this device is designed to deliver. The Amazon Fire HD 10 is arguably the most budget-friendly full-size tablet on the market for streaming, reading and browsing. Storage starts at 32GB and is expandable up to 1TB via a microSD card, giving you plenty of room for downloaded shows, books and apps. Beyond these core specs, the Fire HD 10 includes 5MP front and rear cameras for video calls and casual photos — while it’s not as great as the cameras on the other tablets on this list, it gets the job done. This tablet also comes with hands-free Alexa support, so you can control smart home devices, check the weather or play music with just your voice. How I picked the best tablets To come up with a list of the best tablets, I spoke to Elterman about what to look for when shopping. Below is the criteria he suggested paying attention to. Operating system: An operating system (OS) is the software at the root of your tablet — it manages nearly all its other processes. Your OS also decides what kinds of apps you can download, and what the general interface of your tablet will look like. Different people prefer different OSs — usually it’s easiest to use the same system your other devices use due to familiarity. With that in mind, I included a mix of tablets that use different systems.Size: Part of the convenience of a tablet is how much smaller it is than a laptop. All of the tablets on this list are less than 11 inches long and weigh around a pound, making them easy to carry all day and compact enough to fit in most bags and backpacks. Battery life: Every tablet above has at least 10 hours of battery life, allowing you to use them for most of the day without needing a recharge. How to find the right tablet for you Tablets can cost less than $100 or more than $1,000 and come with all sorts of features. To find the best one for your needs (and essentially budget), keep the following factors in mind: The other devices you use Like your phone and your laptop, your tablet is powered by a specific operating system, typically either Apple’s iPad OS, some version of Android, or Amazon’s Fire OS. When buying a new tablet, it’s important that you pick one that uses the system you are most comfortable with, says Elterman. With your phone, tablet and computer all using the same operating system, you can more easily sync messages and apps to create a more seamless experience between your devices, in my experience. For example, my Apple phone, tablet and laptop all sync together through Apple’s software, allowing me to sync content like messages and photos across all three devices. Your storage needs There’s nothing worse than having to go through your device and delete items after running out of storage space, says Elterman. While you can store your photos on cloud services like iCloud and Google One, they often have monthly subscription fees and are not ideal for storing apps and games. Think about what you are going to use your tablet for. If you are primarily going to stream content, browse the web and hop on video calls, you will not need a large amount of storage space, and can likely opt for the smallest storage option, in my experience. If you are going to be using dozens of apps, downloading games and taking photos and videos, get a model with more than the minimum storage offered. Consider a case and warranty Smartphones, tablets and laptops are all expensive pieces of tech we travel with often. Most of them can benefit from protective gear like a case or screen protector. This is especially true if you have a more expensive tablet like the iPad Pro, as fixing damage can be very pricey, and a case or extended warranty can mitigate those costs, says Elterman. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. articles.title: Benjamin Netanyahu attacks Israel’s enemies and allies in UN speech
articles.summary: Israeli prime minister denounces Iran, NYC Mayor Mamdani and critics accusing Israel of crimes against Palestinians.
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used his platform at the United Nations General Assembly to attack detractors and allies alike, and his presence sparked uproar in the chamber.

Speaking before the UNGA on Thursday, Netanyahu attacked New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, critics and Iran’s leadership, as well as allied countries like the United Kingdom and France.

Back home, the prime minister is locked in a tight race to stay in power ahead of an election on October 27, and analysts say his UNGA speech was aimed as much at people back home as it was at international viewers.

Dozens of envoys from around the world walked out as the speech began, some jeering and booing, while Netanyahu’s own team stood and applauded, and the speaker of the session shouted for order.

“If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t left this hall, please do so now,” Netanyahu said to those turning their backs on him.

He addressed the war that the US and Israel launched on Iran in February, saying: “Devastating Iran’s nuclear facilities was hard, was very hard to do.”

“But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as prime minister”, claiming that if he had not, “we’d all be dead”, he added.

In his own speech before the UNGA on Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also addressed the nuclear issue and called out the “double standard”.

“The nuclear weapon is in Israel, but the inspectors are in Iran. Israel kills, but Iran is subject to sanctions,” Pezeshkian said.

Netanyahu on Thursday said that Israel was fighting a “seven-front war”, including Gaza, the occupied West Bank, Syria, Lebanon, Iran, Yemen’s Houthis and militias in Iraq.

“We are going to win. We have no other choice,” Netanyahu declared, repeating the words of his older brother Yonatan Netanyahu, who was killed in 1976 during Operation Entebbe in Uganda.

The United Kingdom and France, historic partners of Israel, were also in Netanyahu’s firing line. They have become increasingly outspoken in their criticism of the country’s actions and have both imposed limited sanctions on Israeli exports from the occupied West Bank.

“They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he said.

But Netanyahu thanked his “friend”, United States President Donald Trump.

“In this battle against the barbarians, we’ve had no greater partner than President Trump,” he said, as the US delegation joined the Israeli one in applauding Netanyahu’s remark.

“I thank him,” said Netanyahu, adding that Israel and the US had acted together as pilots from both countries “flew joint missions over the skies of Iran”.

Netanyahu said the US and Israel also “worked together to bring back our remaining hostages [from Gaza]”, as he defended Israeli actions in the enclave against charges of genocide.

“To all those spreading lies about my country, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the anti-Semitic mayor of New York, I say this: shame on you,” Netanyahu said as he attacked Zohran Mamdani, who had previously said he would push for the arrest of the Israeli prime minister during his visit to the city.

“Mr Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me. Well, you can’t silence me,” Netanyahu said as he denied that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.

Reacting to Netanyahu’s comments, Mamdani called the accusations against him “baseless lies” meant to “sanitise his genocide of Palestinians”.

Since October 7, 2023, Israel has faced repeated accusations of genocide in Gaza, as well as systematic war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

The Hague-based International Criminal Court (ICC) said in 2024 it had reasonable grounds to believe Netanyahu was responsible for war crimes in Gaza, where over 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Netanyahu denies the ICC charges.

Netanyahu attended the UNGA meeting despite an ICC warrant calling for his arrest. While he was welcomed, the Trump administration denied a visa for Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, who addressed the UNGA through a prerecorded video statement from Ramallah earlier in the day.

As Netanyahu spoke, activists from US-based organisation Jewish Voice for Peace protested outside, accusing the United Nations of “playing host to a war criminal”.

“All across New York, Jews, Palestinians and people of conscience are rising up to demand an end to US support for the livestreamed horrors, rigged ceasefires and forever wars,” Sonya Meyerson-Knox, the group’s communications director, told Al Jazeera.

Meyerson-Knox said that “solidarity with Palestinian freedom has never been greater, and here in the US we are demanding with one voice to stop arming Israel”.

Adding to tensions, dozens of protesters, some brandishing “stop the genocide” banners, gathered near the UN. Several demonstrators were detained, including prominent actor Susan Sarandon.

Inside the UN, but addressing divisions back home in Israel, Netanyahu said: “Throughout this long war, our goal never wavers – to win with unwavering resolve … What unites us is so much stronger: our history, our values, our courage.”

Ariel Cohen, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center, said the Israeli prime minister delivered a “good speech” at the UNGA but that he did so in the “wrong forum”.

“That speech should be given at an election rally in Israel; this is who he’s communicating to,” Cohen told Al Jazeera. “He is making points that should be made to the Israeli audience for his political survival.”

Netanyahu is only making a whirlwind stop in New York before rushing back to Israel, where the election campaign is in full swing. He is not scheduled to meet any top US leaders.

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: Call for a free Iran echoes at the United Nations
articles.summary: Retired Gen. Keith Kellogg and Ambassador Marc Ginsberg called for Iran sanctions at a rally outside the U.N. General Assembly protesting the Iranian president.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS, N.Y. — When Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the United Nations General Assembly, he portrayed his nation as the victim of American and Israeli terrorism. But outside the hall, several thousand protesters chanted that he should be arrested for being a terrorist. "They are terrorists. He is a terrorist," former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani told the gathering. "It is useless to negotiate with them because they are terrorists, murderers, possibly in some ways insane religious maniacs. This would be like trying to reach an agreement with Hitler." Various former high-level government officials struck the same tone, slamming the radical Islamic regime they say has savagely oppressed and butchered the Iranian people for decades. Estimates say upward of 20,000 protestors who took to the streets of Iran earlier this year demanding freedom have been murdered by the government. Reports of executions of political prisoners continue each week. "It is time now to free Iran from the mullahs," Retired Lt. General Keith Kellogg, who has served in both Trump administrations, told the gathering, "You have a road map to a secular, non-nuclear Republic of Iran, one that rejoins the free world as a friend." TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH Former U.S. Ambassador Marc Ginsberg urged Congress to pass the Maximum Support Act, legislation that would crack down on Iran's resources, confiscate assets of the government and support internet freedom so the Iranian people could organize and have a voice. "All you have to do, President Trump, is to provide the funding and the support that we need, the tools the Iranian people need," Ginsberg said. "That is the type of help you promised. "The people of Iran have rejected every form of dictatorship, whether religious or monarchical," Maryam Rajavi said in a video message to the rally. She is president-elect of the group that sponsored the protest, the National Council of Resistance of Iran. "The voice of protest from Iran's oppressed people is being heard. The voice rejects the continued occupation of Iran's seat by religious fanatics," she said, referring to the regime's membership in the world body. US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS The rally was held over a two-day period, and the message to the United Nations diplomats remained consistent. "The regime only responds to firmness and decisiveness. And that's why sanctions and putting pressure on Iran has been the only solution in terms of external pressure," Alireza Jafarzadeh, deputy director of the NCRI Washington, D.C., office told Fox News. "The regime is incapable of reform and change. If they were able, they would have done it a long time ago. The real solution for Iran is change by the people of Iran. They can have any talks, any concessions, none of that is going to change the behavior of the regime. articles.title: Hurricane Polo drenches Mexico coast as Tropical Storm Nolo threatens Hawaii with heavy rain
articles.summary: Powerful Hurricane Polo battered Mexico’s Pacific coast with heavy rain and flooding on Thursday, while Tropical Storm Nolo strengthened south of Hawaii
articles.body: Powerful Hurricane Polo battered Mexico’s Pacific coast with heavy rain and flooding on Thursday, while Tropical Storm Nolo strengthened south of Hawaii and threatened to bring potentially dangerous rainfall, flooding and landslides to the islands.The US National Hurricane Center warned that Polo could trigger life-threatening flooding and landslides along Mexico’s western coast. In the port city of Lazaro Cardenas, seawater swept into homes, leaving furniture and wooden debris scattered across streets.Mexican authorities opened shelters, evacuated residents from vulnerable areas and deployed 15,000 security personnel along the coast as Polo moved offshore.Meanwhile, Nolo was gaining strength south of Hawaii’s Big Island, with forecasters expecting the storm to become a hurricane. Heavy rain was forecast to begin affecting Hawaii on Thursday, with hurricane-force winds possible by early Saturday.Polo brings flooding threat to MexicoPolo has fluctuated between Category 4 and Category 5 strength, both classified as major hurricanes. Its strongest winds were expected to remain offshore as the centre of the storm passed near Mexico’s Pacific coast before moving back out to sea.The hurricane centre warned that Guerrero and Michoacan faced the greatest risk, particularly rural and mountainous areas where flooding and mudslides could become dangerous.Tropical-storm-force winds extended up to 125 miles (201 kilometres) from Polo’s centre. Although the storm was expected to move away from land, forecasters said it could turn back toward Mexico’s coast farther north on Saturday.Authorities suspended schools as a precaution and moved residents from high-risk areas to shelters. The number of people evacuated was not immediately available.The storm brought back memories of previous hurricanes that devastated Mexico’s Pacific coast, including Hurricane Otis, which struck Acapulco in 2023 and left the city severely damaged.“So many people said it wouldn’t happen and then it did. After that, you’re left on edge,” said Gonzalo Ramírez, a bartender in the city.Hawaii braces for NoloFar south of Hawaii’s Big Island, Tropical Storm Nolo was strengthening and could become a hurricane as early as Friday.Forecasters warned that Nolo could bring more than 2 feet (60 centimetres) of rain to parts of Hawaii. The Big Island was expected to receive the heaviest rainfall, with forecasts indicating up to 20 inches (50 centimetres) in some areas and potentially higher totals through Saturday.Maui was also at risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.John Bravender, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Honolulu, said the storm’s exact path remained uncertain but expressed concern about the southeastern Big Island, where the ground remained saturated following recent storms.“There are several communities that were isolated, flooded, roads that were washed out,” he said. “It’s that same area that is most under threat,” Bravender said.Bravender said the frequency of storms affecting Hawaii this year was unusual.“In my 20 years of experience here, I’ve never seen three hurricane watches for the islands in the same year,” said John Bravender of the National Weather Service in Honolulu.Hawaii has already faced major flooding, an earthquake and two hurricanes since mid-August.Hawaii activates emergency measuresHawaii Governor Josh Green issued an emergency proclamation as officials prepared for Nolo. More than 230 Hawaii National Guard members were activated, while schools were closed for the remainder of the week.Officials urged residents to prepare emergency kits and make arrangements for possible flooding and disruptions.Hawaiian Electric said crews that had been helping restore electricity on Kauai following Hurricane Lowell would return to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island ahead of Nolo.El Niño linked to Pacific storm activityThe series of storms comes as El Niño drives changes in weather patterns across the world. The climate phenomenon can contribute to drought in some regions while increasing rainfall and flooding in others.El Niño typically suppresses Atlantic hurricane activity but can increase tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific by creating conditions with more moisture and less wind shear.Two other storms remain away from landHurricane Odalys, another Pacific storm, was located about 1,110 miles (1,785 kilometres) west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and posed no immediate threat to land.In the northern Atlantic, Tropical Storm Fay re-formed early Thursday, according to the US hurricane centre. It was located nearly 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometres) west-southwest of the Azores.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Massachusetts car dealer bought a Nantucket cottage for $899,000, said ‘if I get five years out of it, I’m good’; five years later, the 1951 home sits just feet from a 40-foot drop into the Atlantic
articles.summary: When Charles Fotopoulos bought a small cottage on Nantucket’s Sconset Bluff in September 2021, he knew the property came with a serious risk: the Atlantic
articles.body: When Charles Fotopoulos bought a small cottage on Nantucket’s Sconset Bluff in September 2021, he knew the property came with a serious risk: the Atlantic Ocean was steadily eating away at the land beneath it.Fotopoulos, a Massachusetts car dealer, and his wife, Miglena, paid $899,000 for 93 Baxter Road, a 1951 cottage perched near the edge of the bluff. The price was notably low for Nantucket, where luxury properties can sell for many millions of dollars.Five years later, the cottage remains standing. But the amount of land separating it from the edge of the bluff has become extremely small.According to the Nantucket Current, only a few feet of ground now separate the rear of the home from a roughly 40-foot drop to the beach below. When the cottage was built, the ocean was hundreds of yards away.He knew the risks before buyingFotopoulos did not hide the reason he was willing to take the gamble.“It was cheap and I said ‘hey, I’ll buy it’,” he told the Nantucket Current after the 2021 purchase. He said he believed the foundation was structurally sound and that the geotubes protecting the bluff could help keep the property safe.“If I get five years out of it, I think I’m good. I’ll take that any day,” he said.The property’s location also offered something difficult to put a price on: an unobstructed view of the Atlantic.“It’s both a great view, and a scary view,” Fotopoulos said.That combination has defined the cottage’s recent history.The previous owners also tried to save itSteven and Erin Freeman purchased the property for $1.53 million in 2007, when an estimated 50 to 70 feet of land separated the cottage from the bluff’s edge.They eventually sold it to the Fotopouloses for $899,000, taking a loss of roughly $631,000 on the sale price alone.The Freemans had previously taken steps to protect the property. In 2010, they moved the house farther back toward Baxter Road. In 2017, they also carried out work to reinforce the top of the bluff. The work was not approved by Nantucket’s Conservation Commission, which later issued an enforcement order.The couple were also involved with the Sconset Beach Preservation Fund, a group of property owners that has supported the use of geotubes along the coastline.Real estate broker Jamie Howarth said the buyers understood what they were getting into.“They knew the risks going in,” Howarth told the Nantucket Current in 2021. “I was clear with him and we were clear with him that there was serious risk.”The cottage has also been used as a rentalDespite the erosion concerns, the property has continued to generate rental income.Howarth suggested that the Freemans may have recovered some of their financial loss through summer rentals, with peak weeks reportedly reaching as much as $10,000.The new owners appear to have explored the same option. Listing records show the cottage was advertised for rent at $10,000 a month in September 2025. During the most recent summer, it reportedly rented for $29,500 per month.Fotopoulos had previously argued that the property still made financial sense despite its precarious location.“It is what it is. It’s a hole in the ocean on Nantucket. It’s really worth $8 million if you really think about it,” he said, pointing to an $8.4 million comparable property nearby.Today, comparable Nantucket properties with ocean views are listed at prices ranging from about $11.5 million to $29 million.Geotubes remain at the centre of the disputeOne of the main protections for the cottage has been a system of geotubes at the base of the bluff. The large fabric structures are filled with sand and positioned along the shoreline to absorb the force of the waves.They have helped slow erosion in parts of the area, but their presence has also become the subject of a long-running dispute on Nantucket.The Conservation Commission voted in 2021 to have the geotubes removed, while the Sconset Beach Preservation Fund continued fighting to maintain the coastal protection.The debate intensified this year after additional sections of the bluff collapsed.In March, the commission's chair warned that the project could be approaching “complete failure.” A winter storm with wind gusts exceeding 80 mph subsequently removed additional sand from the shoreline.A larger battle over coastal protectionThe cottage at 93 Baxter Road has become part of a wider debate about how Nantucket should respond to coastal erosion and whether structures such as geotubes should be expanded.At Town Meeting this spring, voters narrowly rejected a proposal to extend the coastal protection system by 3,000 feet.A Superior Court judge later sided with the expansion permit in August. Meanwhile, the Conservation Commission indicated that it could allow repairs to a damaged section of the existing system following what officials described as suspected vandalism in January.State environmental regulators also raised concerns about the proposal in an August 31 letter, identifying 12 unresolved issues.The dispute has implications beyond the single cottage. Critics of the coastal armoring project have argued that older homes such as 93 Baxter Road play a role in providing the legal basis for hard coastal protection.“The presence of that pre-1978 house is what provides the legal justification, in part, for the permitting of hard armoring,” Nantucket Coastal Conservancy’s D. Anne Atherton said around the time of the 2021 sale.The Fotopouloses have no connection to the preservation group.Five years later, the cottage is still thereWhen Fotopoulos purchased 93 Baxter Road, he said he would be satisfied if the cottage survived for five years.That five-year mark has now arrived, but the landscape around the house has changed dramatically. The bluff has continued to retreat, leaving only a narrow strip of land between the cottage and the drop to the beach.For Fotopoulos, the uncertainty remains part of owning the property.“How long does it last? You and I don’t know that,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: AOC's 'Tax the Rich' designer accused of leaving small business with massive charity gala bill
articles.summary: Aurora James, the designer behind AOC's "Tax the Rich" Met Gala dress, faces a lawsuit alleging she stiffed a small business out of over $1 million.
articles.body: The fashion designer behind Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's "Tax the Rich" Met Gala dress is facing a seven-figure lawsuit accusing her of stiffing the small business she hired to throw her own star-studded charity gala. According to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital, designer Aurora James, 42, is being sued by event organizer The Gathery Inc. over allegations stemming from unpaid bills after it produced the Fifteen Percent Pledge Gala 2026 at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles earlier this year. The February bash boasted an attendee list that included Meghan Markle and Kimora Lee Simmons and was held with the intention of raising money for Black business owners. ANNA WINTOUR REPORTEDLY FACES CALLS TO RETIRE AFTER JOHN GALLIANO MET GALA FIRESTORM: ‘LOST HER TOUCH’ However, a lawsuit filed in New York Supreme Court by The Gathery alleges James, her nonprofit Fifteen Percent Pledge and its fiscal sponsor, Philanthropic Ventures Foundation (PVF), left the planners with the bill. The plaintiffs are seeking at least $1,082,965 in damages from the three parties, along with contractually owed interest and additional financial damages. According to court documents, James’ nonprofit allegedly made two initial deposits toward the $1.5 million bill to The Gathery, which produced the annual fundraiser in both 2024 and 2025 without issue, before ceasing all payments in November 2025. James "personally directed the project and repeatedly induced TGI to continue performing even after payment defaults had begun," the suit states. PRINCE HARRY SUED BY CHARITY HE FOUNDED IN HONOR OF PRINCESS DIANA "James approved change orders expanding the scope and cost of the event, signed the Feb. 4, 2026, amendment admitting breach, and assured TGI that payment would be forthcoming — all while knowing, or recklessly disregarding, that 15PP lacked the ability to pay," it continued. James founded the nonprofit organization in 2020 in response to the murder of George Floyd with a goal of encouraging retailers to dedicate 15% of their storefront’s shelf space to products created by Black-owned businesses. According to its website, Fifteen Percent Pledge is a self-described "racial equity and economic justice non-profit organization working toward a more equitable economic future." "Launched in 2020 by Aurora James, the initiative was born from seeing multiple acts of injustice and police brutality in the United States with a lack of accountability for the systemic issues at play," its website states. DEFEATED PROGRESSIVE ‘SQUAD’ LAWMAKER IN HOT SEAT FOR NON-PROFIT’S MISSING PAPER TRAIL The ongoing lawsuit is not James’ first time allegedly missing payments. James, who shares a son with Benjamin Bronfman, son of music executive Edgar Bronfman Jr. and actress Sherry Brewer, was reported in 2021 to have run up tax debts through Cultural Brokerage Agency, the parent company of her Brother Vellies fashion brand, including three open state tax warrants from 2018-19 totaling $14,798 in unpaid employee withholding and 15 warrants since 2015, according to the New York Post. The company has also reportedly faced multiple legal claims alleging it repeatedly failed to pay worker benefits. The alleged financial hypocrisy by James, an outspoken activist with deep ties to the fashion world, was noted by both legal and political experts. "These are still allegations that have to be proven in court, but there’s an undeniable irony in an organization dedicated to supporting small businesses being accused of stiffing one for more than $1 million," former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told Fox News Digital. "If you preach economic fairness, you have to practice it too." AOC DOUBLES DOWN ON ‘MYTH’ OF EARNING A BILLION DOLLARS, CLAIMS FORTUNES ARE BUILT ON ‘ABUSE’ Kaivon Shroff, a former digital organizer for Hillary Clinton’s campaign, also noted the apparent irony in the allegations against James. "AOC made Aurora James’s ‘Tax the Rich’ dress one of the defining political images of the Met Gala and excess wealth at a time of great economic inequality, so the irony here is impossible to miss," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "James built her public brand around economic justice and supporting Black-owned businesses," he added, noting that she is being sued by a small business. "That is exactly the kind of contradiction opponents seize on to argue that the politics are performative. "Movements built around economic fairness and supporting marginalized businesses are so important, and they depend heavily on credibility and goodwill," he added. "When the people most visibly associated with those causes are accused of behaving in ways that seem completely at odds with the message, the damage does not stop with the individual. It gives critics an easy way to discredit the cause itself." articles.title: 'We're all broke': Would you chase a friend for £5?
articles.summary: What's the smallest amount of money you would ask a friend to pay you back?
articles.body:
You pick up the bill for dinner, pay for the taxi home or grab a friend's coffee with the promise they'll pay you back later, but days go by and the money never arrives.

At what point do you ask them for it again and how small is too small to chase?

For some, $5 (£3.70) is worth a reminder, while for others, asking a friend to repay anything under $20 (£15) feels more awkward than simply taking the hit.

Henry Payne says he's "sent a request for $8.50, but I wouldn't go lower than $8".

The 21-year-old New Yorker adds that he will chase someone once but "two requests is insane".

"I would rather swallow the $8.50 than send another request."

He does admit that he's sometimes the person on the other side of the transaction and can be forgetful himself.

"For everyone that I haven't sent back money to, I just forgot, feel free to double request me."

Kaz Jahanbini, 19, says needing to ask to be paid back in the first place can be frustrating.

"If someone bought me something, I'm immediately paying them back. So then I'm thinking for them, what's the delay?"

His rule for navigating friendship and finances is to "keep your wallet close but your friends closer".

His friend Nouria agrees and says as a student "every extra dollar counts" but she would usually only ask for money back from a friend if it was more than $10.

A recent study found that 76% of Gen Z who have fronted money for a group expense, like a trip or event, say they were not fully repaid, and 55% say it created tension or negatively affected a relationship.

For British student Betsie Brooke-Taylor, 19, the threshold to ask for money back is a fiver as she says "every little helps".

She sees a cultural difference between the UK and US and even though "we are all broke, I think Americans are a bit more generous".

Betsie also thinks technology makes settling small debts easier in the US, where payment apps such as Venmo are widely used.

Venmo lets users send and request money through an app which includes the function of sending a reminder if someone hasn't paid you. In the US, more than 95 million people have a Venmo account .

"In the UK you have to ask for the account number and sort code, and not everyone has that on hand," she says.

For 19-year-old Annika Violet, the amount she would ask back from a friend depends on whether she's consistently paying for them.

"I prefer to do something where I get them this time and they get me next time but if I'm consistently paying and you're not, then I will request the $5."

Unlike many, Annika doesn't find money conversations uncomfortable.

"I am so confrontational, I do not find it awkward. If you're my friend, you would pay me back."

Annika's friend Hanako Stepper says she finds it awkward asking for money but wishes she didn't.

"I've never chased anyone - I'm just sad if I don't get paid back."

Annika's advice to those who do struggle to ask is to "be brave and bold".

"If they are going to give you flak about it, maybe it's a sign they are not a good friend."

How do you ask for money back without making it awkward?

Money expert Laura Pomfret says many people feel embarrassed about asking to be paid back, and Britons in particular can find it awkward.

"We're often very British about asking for money back," she says, suggesting people may be worried about being judged as a "cheapskate".

Her top tips for asking friends to pay up are:

She adds that you shouldn't convince yourself that a debt is too small to justify asking for it as "if you want the money paid back then the amount shouldn't matter".

And if the same friend repeatedly fails to pay, Pomfret suggests remembering it the next time you're about to pay for them and think twice.

Several people the BBC spoke to said the amount itself mattered less when somebody repeatedly failed to pay.

New York student Ella Feuille, 21, says $15 is roughly the point at which she would consider requesting money.

If a significant amount was owed, Ella says she would ask around three times before giving up but wouldn't necessarily forget about it.

"I have friends who I know now it has to go on their card because they're not going to pay me back."

Her friend Katrina Dimingot agrees and says she much prefers a method where "we don't pay each other back, we just take it in turns to get things for each other".

articles.title: It’s cute. It’s cuddly. And it wants all your data.
articles.summary: Meta is touting its new personal AI agent, Muse, as a product “built for everyone” — including those who lack experience with technology.
articles.body: Meta hopes its new AI agent will win people over by being cute. Muse, the tech giant’s cuddly, doll-like AI agent, shot to the top of the Apple App Store charts after it was featured this week at the company’s Meta Connect conference. The company is touting the tool, designed to help people with their everyday tasks, as an AI agent “built for everyone,” including those who lack experience with technology. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the default Muse avatar, which is cream-colored and has beady black eyes and an upward smile, is named “Jolly,” for its “jolly and completely customizable character and personality.” Muse is being launched as tech companies seek to make their AI-powered products more palatable to humans, often by giving them cute, almost petlike appearances, voices and personalities. Experts have said design choices that humanize technology may become more common as robot-human interaction grows more prevalent in everyday spaces, as cuteness evokes “deep-seated biological responses” in people. “It was only about six months ago that having a personal agent running on your own computer was the sign of someone who is completely AI-pilled and thinking nonstop about agents,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, said Wednesday. “But for that small group of nerds ... it looked like the beginning of personal superintelligence. And today with Muse, we’ve brought that magic to everyone.” Muse agents can take on a variety of appearances, with users able to customize everything from their names to their attire. Zuckerberg’s agent, which wears a toga and a wreath around its head, is named Agrippa, after the Roman general and statesman. During the event, Zuckerberg also teased what he calls the “Muse charm,” a small handheld device that can activate the agent on the go. He raised the keychain charm onstage at Meta Connect in Menlo Park, California, showing off what looks like a blend of a Labubu and a Tamagotchi. “Talking to your Muse is often the fastest way to get things done, and it is also just really fun and cute,” he said, saying he used Agrippa to come up with a baking recipe and order ingredients for him and his daughter. Muse is also being integrated directly into Meta’s expanding lineup of AI-powered glasses, which have been criticized over fears of casual surveillance. Zuckerberg has told NBC News that Meta will continue to bolster privacy safeguards for its smart glasses. Zuckerberg said every Muse agent has its own private and secure computer called Muse Secure VM, a dedicated secure computer that houses both the agent and the user’s personal data. Down the line, he said, Meta plans to release Muse Confidential VM “so that even Meta won’t be able to see that information.” “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives,” he said. Online, the reaction has been mixed. Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted a flurry of memes inserting Muse into moments from movies, shows and historical events. Some followed his lead by making their own avatars and sharing screenshots on social media. Others, however, expressed skepticism, citing security concerns. “Am I the only one who doesn’t want to let meta have access to my whole life?” a user posted. “We are going to need some tight defenses and 3rd party testing of these platforms... like all software products,” entrepreneur and angel investor Jason Calacanis wrote. Zuckerberg has continued to be bullish on AI despite recent calls from tech executives and government officials to pump the brakes on AI development amid surging fears about the existential risk the technology poses. He shared his thoughts recently on X, saying market forces should be enough to keep AI companies in line. “My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind,” he wrote, adding: “Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would.”

articles.title: Iran’s president claims Supreme Leader Khamenei healthy, able to govern
articles.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed Thursday that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has been absent from public view for months, is “completely” healthy despite reports that he could be deceased or brain-dead. Questions have surrounded Khamenei’s condition since he was reportedly seriously injured during U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Feb. 28 that killed his father and predecessor,…
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed Thursday that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has been absent from public view for months, is “completely” healthy despite reports that he could be deceased or brain-dead.

Questions have surrounded Khamenei’s condition since he was reportedly seriously injured during U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Feb. 28 that killed his father and predecessor, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along with several members of his family.

The younger Khamenei is believed to have gone into hiding and has not been seen in public or photographed since becoming the regime’s next supreme leader.

When asked by Fox News’s “Special Report” host Bret Baier when the last time Pezeshkian saw Khamenei in-person, the Iranian president said the two met “about a month ago” and had “conducted talks.”

“I don’t remember the dates. About a month, a month and a half ago,” Pezeshkian said. “We met for about seven hours.”

Baier asked for a health update on Khamenei and whether he would be able to govern.

“Very much so, completely,” Pezeshkian responded, adding that his administration is being consulted and directed by Khamenei.

When pressed about why the supreme leader has yet to address the public since the start of the war, Pezeshkian blamed Khamenei’s reclusiveness on the “lack of security that was created by the action of foreigners,” whom he called “aggressors.”

Questions have surrounded Khamenei’s condition since he was reportedly seriously injured during Operation Epic Fury that killed his father and predecessor, along with several members of his family.

A report from The Atlantic cited sources in Tehran that speculated Khamenei was either dead or brain-dead, while others believed he was still alive.

President Trump pushed back on the report, saying he doesn’t believe the supreme leader is dead.

“He was very seriously wounded, but I don’t think he’s dead,” he said in an interview with conservative commentator Glenn Beck.

“And if he is, they’re putting on a pretty good show because they talk about going back to talk to him all the time to get a final blessing on things,” Trump added.

The president said Khamenei had suffered very serious wounds in the strikes to “the left side of his body, the arm, the leg, the whole thing.”

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands expected in Paris for Pope Leo's visit
articles.summary: The highpoint of his time in Paris will be a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV embarks on a four-day visit to France on Friday, with the highpoint being a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in central Paris.

For Saturday's afternoon celebration, an altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde and a large area around the Champs-Élysées sealed off by police.

Some 600,000 Catholic faithful are expected to cram the avenue up to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.

Large crowds are also due at other stages in the Pope's itinerary, reflecting an enthusiasm that the Church attributes to growing spiritual thirst among the French and other Europeans.

President Emmanuel Macron will greet the Pope at Orly airport on Friday morning, and then hold talks with him at the Élysée Palace on geopolitical issues and artificial intelligence (AI). He will also deliver a speech with the Pope in Metz.

However, the president will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.

Instead, the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by his wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also due, including Marine Le Pen of the nationalist right, centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, and conservative Bruno Retailleau.

There were reports of tensions between Macron and the Vatican team sent to make arrangements, with the president allegedly frustrated in his wish for a more ceremonial aspect to the visit.

This was dismissed this week by Élysée officials, who said it was customary to offer a visiting head of state – which the Pope is – a range of high-profile events, such as a cavalry escort down the Champs-Élysées. But they said it was never expected that the Pope would actually take the offer up.

They did confirm that Pope Leo turned down Macron's idea of a meeting with artisans who helped rebuild the fire-devastated Notre-Dame cathedral. This was because his agenda was too tight, they said.

After a Popemobile ride through crowds to Notre-Dame cathedral on Friday afternoon, Pope Leo XIV will be joined in the evening by 80,000 young people at the Stade de France in northern Paris.

On Sunday 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes.

On Monday the Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification.

The Pope will also meet a group of migrants in Paris, and in Lourdes some victims of sexual abuse by members of the Catholic clergy.

Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name.

In fact his paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden-name.

France has a historically complex relationship with the Catholic Church of Rome. The country was long known as the "Eldest Daughter of the Church" because supposedly, but inaccurately, it was the first kingdom to convert to Christianity. Actually Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia preceded it.

In the 14th Century the papacy came in exile to Avignon in southern France, and over following centuries French armies periodically intervened in Italian politics, where popes were secular rulers as well as heads of the Church.

Recent popes have all come to France, most notably John-Paul II, who came several times between 1980 and 2004, and Pope Francis who came three times, but avoided Paris, going instead to Strasbourg, Marseilles and Corsica.

Today France has secularised with the rest of Europe, and less than half of the population identifies as Catholic.

The number of regular worshippers has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.

But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.

"France has indeed secularised, but there is a void where God and values used to be," said Cardinal François Bustillo, Bishop of Ajaccio.

"People are searching for something. Maybe they go to India or Tibet or the Amazon. And now the Pope comes here from Rome, bringing a reminder to people of their own roots.

"It was John-Paul II who awoke the East. Now Leo XIV will awake the West," he said.

articles.title: Costa Rica minister fired for unapproved meeting with Trump in US
articles.summary: President Fernandez dismisses foreign minister over his attendance at the “Shield of the Americas” meeting in New York.
articles.body:
Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez has fired Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar after he attended a US-led regional security summit with United States President Donald Trump without notifying her, an omission the government has said blocked her own participation and caused major strategic harm to the country’s interests.

Fernandez said that she should have been the one to attend the meeting of Trump’s anti-cartel “ Shield of the Americas ” alliance in New York. The coalition says its mission is to combat drug trafficking and organised crime across the region.

Tovar attended “without giving prior notice or informing” the president, a conservative Trump ally, of his participation, Costa Rica’s government said.

Several right-wing Latin American presidents also participated in the meeting, which took place on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Fifteen coalition members issued a joint statement declaring their intent to impose asset freezes and visa restrictions and seek criminal liability for members and supporters of 24 criminal organisations.

The gathering was the administration’s latest effort to rally the region behind a more aggressive approach to drug trafficking. Since returning to office last year, Trump has designated cartels as foreign “terrorist” organisations and ordered dozens of strikes on boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific that US officials say were carrying narcotics bound for the US.

Costa Rica, a tourist haven that has long been seen as a beacon of stability in Latin America, is grappling with a surge in drug-related violence.

Tovar avoided commenting on his dismissal and simply thanked Fernandez, in power since last May, for including him in her cabinet.

Indiana Trejos, Costa Rica’s current Minister of Foreign Trade, has been named acting foreign minister and will assume the role upon returning from her mission at the UNGA.

articles.title: Angh by Theja Rio at Toronto: The Indian film taking Nagaland to global cinema
articles.summary: After a major win at Toronto, Angh, a film from northeastern India, is now on a path towards the Oscars.
articles.body:
There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.

The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's northeastern frontier, and is in Konyak, a tribal language unfamiliar to most Indians, never mind audiences abroad. It was director Theja Rio's first feature and most of its cast faced a camera for the first time.

And yet, at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, this quiet film won the Platform Prize, a major juried award.

The award is intended to recognise films with a particularly distinctive directorial voice. The jury praised Rio's "refreshing perspective" and the film's portrait of a world rarely encountered on the international screen.

The win also gives Angh an unusual route towards the 2027 Academy Awards. Under new rules, winners of designated prizes at six international festivals can qualify for consideration in the International Feature Film category without relying solely on their country's official submission.

This does not make Angh an Oscar nominee. But it does place a Konyak-language film from one of India's smallest states inside a global conversation from which such stories have been almost entirely absent.

Rio still sounds slightly startled by it. When we speak in Delhi, roughly 72 hours after the win, he has barely had a moment to breathe - Toronto, flights, interviews, more interviews.

"There were a lot of good films in the competition", he says, including films by far more seasoned directors. His producers were confident.

"They thought we were going to win. I wasn't."

He is also less solemn than Angh might suggest. Before cinema, he wanted to be a rapper - "a kid from Compton instead of a kid from Nagaland", as he puts it. His tastes still range happily from Black Thought, the lead rapper of American hip-hop group The Roots, to his favourite filmmaker, the Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami.

But for his first feature, he turned close to home.

Set in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba, the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village, and his young son, as the world around them changes. The Konyaks are one of Nagaland's 17 major tribes, concentrated in the eastern district of Mon, where such chiefs are known as Anghs. Even today, some older men bear facial tattoos associated with the Konyaks' historical practice of headhunting.

Anghba and his son are among the last in their region to hold to an ancestral faith as Christianity spreads.

Then an American missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall, arrives. The father resists but the son is now curious.

Rio says the idea for the film came a few years ago, when he was visiting Mon for another project. What struck him was how closely different generations seemed to live alongside one another there.

Within a single family, he says, a grandfather might be a former headhunter, his face still tattooed; two generations later, his grandson might play guitar in a rock band.

"It feels like you've jumped on a time machine," Rio says. "The past and the present sort of coexist together."

The year also matters. Nagaland, which was earlier part of Assam state, formally became an Indian state in December 1963, during a period of profound political and social change.

By then, Christianity had been spreading among Naga communities for decades, bringing changes extending beyond religious belief into customs, rituals and everyday life.

Dr B Amo Konyak, a scholar of Konyak society, says the changes during this period were almost like a disappearance.

Some practices were lost; others "survived in fragments" - in the memories of elders, in family heirlooms. What had once been part of everyday life became heritage.

But Dr Konyak says culture did not simply stop. People carried parts of it into new religious and social worlds. Traditions survived, but changed meaning as they changed form.

It's this moment of transition that Rio wanted to capture.

"The past 50 or 60 years have brought extraordinary churn," he says, widening the distance between generations.

In Angh, he explores this through the relationship between the father and son who "intimately love and care about each other very deeply", even as their worlds begin to pull apart.

Critic Siddhant Adlakha was struck by the ambiguity the film captures. "Progress and tradition can be nonlinear, even entwined," he says, "rather than strictly opposing forces."

The film is yet to reach a wider audience, but its brief trailer offers a glimpse of how Rio constructed this world. Mist hangs over steep green hills; figures move through forests and village paths; fire and lamplight pick faces out of the darkness.

The landscape is beautiful but not merely picturesque - a small world held together by ritual, family and geography, while something larger presses in from beyond its edges.

Adlakha singles out the quiet close-ups of Anghlong Konyak, the first-time actor who plays the chief, and the "gentleness" with which Rio captures his "subdued rage".

What the camera saw mattered almost as much as where it was looking from.

Konyak people have long been viewed from the outside.

Dr Konyak points to explorers, colonial officials, missionaries and photographers drawn to tattooed faces, ornaments, weapons and headhunting, while the lives behind them often receded from view.

Rio was conscious of inheriting that history. "There have been several films and documentaries made about Nagaland," he says, "but these sort of films tend to follow the gaze of the explorer rather than the subject."

With Angh, he wanted to reverse that gaze, asking viewers to "step inside the shoes of these characters".

The change is subtle but consequential. The Konyaks are no longer an exotic remnant of the past, but people living through what Dr Konyak describes as "love, grief, conflict, faith, uncertainty and generational change".

Konyak advisers worked on dialogue, costume and production design, and much of the cast was drawn from first-time Konyak performers. The forest, too, belongs to the people moving through it. Adlakha says Rio treats it "not just as a setting, but as a home with a history", much as an urban filmmaker might treat Mumbai or New York.

Rio and cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz shot Angh on 16mm film, drawing on photographs and footage of missionaries and Naga communities from the 1950s and 60s.

They wanted to recreate the grain, texture and atmosphere of those archival images, while shifting the point of view from outsider to subject.

It was an evocative choice - and a logistical headache.

Unlike digital footage, the exposed film could not simply be reviewed on set. Every four or five days, the cans had to be sent to Mumbai for processing, while the crew carried on shooting without knowing exactly what they had captured.

During a night shoot with Henshall, an old Second World War Jeep was supposed to be driven into frame. It behaved perfectly through rehearsals. But when the cameras began rolling, the engine refused to start. After repeated attempts, the crew managed to capture just one take of the Jeep entering the frame.

"It was a very difficult night," Rio says.

Angh may be Rio's first feature, but its journey places it within a widening map of Indian cinema, especially in the northeast.

Adlakha points to filmmakers such as Assam's Rima Das and Meghalaya's Dominic Sangma whose work, he says, reveals "how complex and multifaceted the idea of Indian cinema happens to be".

Rio thinks Nagaland still remains at the edge of that scene. Its film industry is, as he puts it, "at a very nascent stage", with little of the reach enjoyed by India's established filmmaking centres.

But he hopes some of the attention around Angh travels back with it.

There are, he says, "so many talented filmmakers with so many beautiful stories that are yet to be told".

For now, though, Rio is looking forward to something more ordinary - getting back to Nagaland.

"I want to play football with my friends."
