articles.title: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
articles.summary: Andy Burnham is under pressure to deliver a compelling vision for the country as he steps from the sidelines on to the main stage.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool.

But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event.

Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers.

Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role".

"People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York.

An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter.

The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again".

So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK – which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core.

As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago.

Back then, he declared then that the country had "lost control" of "the essentials" following the Thatcher-era sell off of utilities and that we were all "overpaying for water, housing energy, transport".

He called for a renewed emphasis on technical education and wanted to see a decade of council house building on the scale of the post-war Labour government.

For a politician frequently denounced for "flip flopping" he has been remarkably consistent in recent times.

He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care.

A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform.

Such a move would be supported by about a quarter of his own MPs and would tie in with his leadership campaign promise of "a new politics", focused on "problem solving" rather than "point scoring".

We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon.

And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North.

The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now.

But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now.

After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office.

We are told there will be policy announcements on each day of the conference – starting on Saturday.

Each announcement will have to fit in with the PM's priorities – "putting power in people's hands" - in other words more devolved powers; "growth in every postcode" – such as investment decisions around the country; and help with cost of living.

Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance.

But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later. The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners.

Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular.

The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield.

The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills.

All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday.

With borrowing costs for last month soaring to their second highest level , his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it.

But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality.

Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength.

Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto.

Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce" is real, though not dramatic.

The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now.

Labour strategists will be pleased that Reform UK's share – 21% in YouGov - is the lowest since January 2025, and that Nigel Farage's party is now neck-and-neck with Kemi Badenoch's Conservatives.

One Labour insider told me that Burnham is happy to see a resilient Badenoch, as this blunts Reform support and could point to a split vote on the right at an election.

And new research from YouGov suggests that at the all important constituency level, 63-68% of Lib Dem and Green voters would tactically vote for Labour to stop Reform UK winning their seat.

Burnham of course also faces a challenge on the left.

How much of a threat Zack Polanski's Greens can be in some traditional Labour seats will be tested in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election just a week after the Labour conference concludes.

Downing Street insists that an early election is not being planned.

To say anything else, though, would be to repeat the uncertainty of Gordon Brown's early months in No 10 when election speculation wasn't doused - and had become so rife that he was reputationally damaged when he decided not to go to the polls.

But some who have been in regular touch with No 10 tell me they have seen no serious signs that an early election is in the offing.

Burnham appears determined to give his government enough time in office to present tangible achievements to a sceptical electorate.

And with Labour still well below the 34% vote share it captured in 2024, many Labour MPs will be pushing the PM not to cut and run.

So don't expect the centre point of Burnham's conference speech to be a message to his MPs to go back to their constituencies and prepare for a loss of some of their seats.

But equally don't expect election speculation to subside at this conference.

The Labour Party has tried and trusted methods of managing dissent at party conferences, when it comes to votes on party policy.

But the coming week could see a concerted effort by some on the left to push for a complete ban on arms sales to Israel and for Israel's actions in Gaza to be described by Labour as a genocide.

Those close to Burnham believe he has gained considerable credit by sanctioning the illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank and won't need to go further.

There is also some frustration that his government has not yet revised proposals to make migrants wait much longer to gain permanent residency rights, and there are genuine differences over whether the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields should go ahead.

But while Burnham is facing some difficult calls, this is not a leader facing a restless party in revolt.

He has offered to give the hard-pressed public "breathing space" amid a cost of living crisis.

And his own party is so far giving him breathing space as leader – largely sighing with relief that it is not Sir Keir Starmer who will be delivering the main address this year.

Senior Labour officials have hailed the forthcoming conference as an opportunity to "show voters a party that is boldly, confidently, and authentically Labour".

But not too far below the political radar, there are already demands from some in the wider Labour movement to prove it.

articles.title: Turning Point USA fires back at ICE shooting lawyer over deleted Charlie Kirk post
articles.summary: Turning Point USA's Andrew Kolvet called the ICE shooting victim and his attorney a "perfect match" after her deleted post about Charlie Kirk resurfaced.
articles.body: Turning Point USA (TPUSA) spokesman Andrew Kolvet fired back Thursday at the attorney representing a Venezuelan man shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin, Texas, calling the two a "perfect match" after the lawyer drew criticism over a deleted social media post referencing the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Kolvet, also executive producer of "The Charlie Kirk Show," told Fox News Digital the organization backed the federal immigration officers involved while criticizing attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch and her client, 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez. "We stand with our brave men and women of ICE who are defending American sovereignty and keeping American citizens safe," Kolvet said. "While everyone is entitled to their defense, it's not surprising the quality of lawyer an illegal alien from Venezuela attracts who had a final notice of deportation before leading law enforcement on a dangerous high-speed chase. "They seem a perfect match." REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR Lincoln-Goldfinch drew criticism this week after a since-deleted social media post referencing Kirk resurfaced. In the post, she questioned how someone could resist being shot while invoking Kirk. "How do you resist getting shot in the neck? Does Charlie Kirk have any advice on that?" Lincoln-Goldfinch said in the post. She previously addressed the controversy in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying her office determined the post could be interpreted differently than intended and removed it. "A post referencing the death of Charlie Kirk was removed from our account. We recognized the post could be misconstrued, and that's why it came down. We have also addressed this issue internally," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. HOW CHARLIE KIRK’S ASSASSINATION CHANGED THE WAY CONSERVATIVES APPROACH HOSTILE OPPONENTS The dispute came as new evidence emerged about the ICE operation that ended with Graces Perez being shot. Surveillance footage published Wednesday showed at least two federal law enforcement vehicles pursuing Graces Perez's vehicle with emergency lights flashing and sirens sounding before the shooting. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed the video's authenticity to Fox News Digital. Lincoln-Goldfinch has disputed the federal government’s account, saying Garces Perez was working as a DoorDash driver when an unmarked vehicle struck his car and that he did not initially know federal agents were pursuing him. She has also challenged DHS’ characterization of his immigration status. DHS said Garces Perez is a Venezuelan national who had a final order of removal and was the subject of a targeted vehicle stop. The department also said his work authorization had expired in 2025 and disputed claims about his treatment after the shooting. "No amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job to arrest illegal aliens from our communities," DHS said. AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARKS FIGHT OVER VENEZUELAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S DEPORTATION Austin police released body camera footage Tuesday showing officers arriving immediately after the shooting and helping Graces Perez from his vehicle. The video contradicted an earlier claim that federal agents pulled him from the car, although the videos did not capture the shooting itself. The shooting has also moved into federal court. Lincoln-Goldfinch’s firm filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Garces Perez’s immediate removal, and a federal judge ordered that he remain in the country so he can appear at a Sept. 30 hearing. The circumstances surrounding the shooting remain under investigation. Homeland Security Investigations, with assistance from the FBI, is leading the federal investigation, while Austin authorities have also reviewed evidence surrounding the encounter. articles.title: D4vd murder case: Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s family breaks silence as legal battle begins
articles.summary: The family of Celeste Rivas Hernandez is speaking publicly about their daughter after singer D4vd was charged in connection with the 14-year-old’s death.
articles.body: The family of Celeste Rivas Hernandez is speaking publicly about their daughter after singer D4vd was charged in connection with the 14-year-old’s death. Their statement focuses less on the details surrounding the criminal case and more on the girl they remember at home: a daughter who loved music, dancing and spending Friday nights with her family.Celeste Rivas Hernandez family remembers their daughterCeleste’s parents, Jesus Rivas and Mercedes Martinez, released a statement through their attorney after D4vd, whose legal name is David Burke, was charged with first-degree murder."Celeste was a beautiful, strong girl who loved to sing and dance."Her parents also recalled simple family moments that now carry painful meaning."Every Friday night was movie night and we spent wonderful times together.""We love her very much and she always told us that she loved us. We miss her deeply," the statement continued. "All we want is justice for Celeste."The family attended D4vd’s first court appearance following his arrest. Their attorney, Patrick Steinfeld, said the family wants Celeste’s memory honoured and her voice heard throughout the legal process.The case began attracting widespread attention in September 2025, when authorities found Celeste’s remains inside a Tesla at a Hollywood tow yard. Police said the vehicle had been abandoned and later impounded. Investigators found the teenager’s remains after officers were called over an unpleasant smell coming from the vehicle.Authorities said Celeste had last been known to be alive on April 23, 2025. Police have described her as a reported runaway from Riverside County.D4vd murder case moves forward in courtD4vd was arrested after a lengthy investigation and charged with first-degree murder. Prosecutors have also filed additional allegations involving sexual acts involving the teenager, mutilation of human remains and an alleged financial motive connected to the singer’s career.Those claims remain allegations, and D4vd has not been convicted. A not guilty plea was entered on his behalf during his arraignment, and he remains in custody without bail.D4vd’s lawyers have firmly denied that he killed Celeste."The actual evidence in this case will show that David Burke did not murder Celeste Rivas Hernandez and he was not the cause of her death," his attorneys Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement on Monday. "We will vigorously defend David's innocence."The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner has determined how Celeste died, according to prosecutors, but those findings remain sealed. articles.summary: US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House on Thursday for
articles.body: US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House on Thursday for a state dinner bringing together a wide cross-section of American business, technology, media and political figures.Xi and Trump entered the White House ahead of the dinner, where both leaders are expected to deliver remarks before joining guests for a meal featuring squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta.Among the high-profile technology executives attending are Apple CEO Tim Cook, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan and TikTok investor Jeff Yass.The guest list also includes senior figures from the US financial sector, including the CEOs of JPMorgan Chase, BlackRock and Goldman Sachs. LVMH CEO Bernard Arnault and Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla are also attending.Fox News hosts Bret Baier and Laura Ingraham are among the media personalities at the dinner, while Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also present.Xi and Trump enter White House for dinnerXi and Peng returned to the White House for the dinner and were welcomed by Trump and Melania Trump.Trump has repeatedly described his relationship with Xi in warm terms during the Chinese leader’s visit, including saying that the two have a “great friendship”.The dinner also reflects the importance Trump has placed on business and technology ties during Xi’s visit, with executives from some of the world's biggest technology companies joining the Chinese delegation and US leadership.Anthropic absent from tech-heavy guest listDespite the presence of executives from OpenAI, Apple, Meta, X, Amazon, Google and Nvidia, Anthropic is notably absent from the guest list, according to BBC.Anthropic is one of the major US artificial intelligence companies and has taken a more cautious position on AI risks and China.Its CEO, Dario Amodei, has previously warned that China taking the lead in artificial intelligence could pose a “grave danger” to the US and the wider world. China has rejected such arguments, with its foreign ministry saying narratives about a Chinese “threat” could undermine international cooperation on AI governance.Democrats criticise summit over Taiwan, tradeThe dinner comes amid criticism from Democratic lawmakers who have accused the Trump administration of putting “pageantry” ahead of substantive issues in its engagement with Beijing.In a statement signed by 19 of the 47 members of the Democratic caucus, the lawmakers urged Trump to immediately provide billions of dollars in aid and arms sales to Taiwan and seek the release of Americans they described as wrongfully detained.They also criticised Trump's decision to loosen restrictions on sales of advanced chips to China.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is among the technology executives attending the dinner.Dinner comes amid US-China tensionsThe high-profile gathering comes against the backdrop of unresolved disagreements between Washington and Beijing over trade, Taiwan, artificial intelligence, advanced technology and critical minerals.While the state dinner offers a public display of diplomatic warmth, the two countries continue to compete over several strategic and economic issues.Trump and Xi are expected to use the visit to discuss those differences while presenting a more cordial public face during the White House dinner.You use AI every day. articles.title: Argentina’s poverty rises to 32 percent under Milei with more pain forecast
articles.summary: A 4.1-percentage-point rise in poverty in the first half of 2026 could be bad news for Milei’s re-election bid.
articles.body:
Argentina’s poverty rate has risen, hitting 32.3 percent in the first half of 2026 under President Javier Milei, partly erasing the country’s earlier gains.

According to figures released by the national statistics agency INDEC on Thursday, the poverty rate rose 4.1 percentage points between January and June compared with the last half of 2025, moving from 28.2 to 32.3 percent.

Extreme poverty — where households cannot afford basic food needs — also rose from 6.3 to 7.5 percent.

More Argentinians found themselves out of work in the second quarter after unemployment rose to 7.9 percent, the country’s highest level since 2021. For many who remain employed, their wages have struggled to keep up with the rising cost of basic goods and services.

Household income per person rose 11.5 percent in the first six months of the year, but the cost of necessities used to calculate the poverty line rose nearly 20 percent, according to INDEC.

The economic pain is expected to worsen.

Estimates from the Catholic University of Argentina (UCA), widely seen as an early indicator of official poverty trends, suggest the poverty rate could rise to 35 percent by the end of the year.

The news comes after Milei, elected in 2023, repeatedly touted declining poverty as evidence that his free-market economic overhaul was bearing fruit.

Poverty surged to nearly 53 percent in the first half of 2024 after his government’s devaluation of the peso and sweeping spending cuts sharply reduced purchasing power. But the rate then fell rapidly as Milei’s austerity drive eased inflation, reaching 28.2 percent in the second half of 2025, the lowest level since early 2018.

Even with this year’s rise, the poverty rate remains below the level reached in the first half of 2024, Milei’s first year in office, when it exceeded 50 percent.

Analysts say it could signal that social gains driven by slowing inflation are losing momentum, with further progress increasingly dependent on stronger job creation and real wage growth.

Average salaries are still below where they stood in real terms when Milei took office in December 2023.

“A modest increase in poverty would not undo the large decline seen under Milei, but it would suggest that the easier part of the improvement has run its course,” Nicholas Watson, managing director for Latin America at consultancy Teneo, said.

Rising hardship appears to be damaging Milei’s support among lower-income voters as he seeks re-election in 2027.

The latest opinion polls suggest his approval rating has fallen sharply among poorer respondents surveyed, raising questions about whether he can retain a constituency that was central to his previous election victory.

A September AtlasIntel survey found disapproval among lower-income respondents, defined as those earning up to about $650 a month, had climbed to nearly 70 percent, while approval fell below 30 percent. A year earlier, those figures stood at 57 percent and 37 percent, respectively.

articles.title: Michigan nurse accused of breaking bones and bruising premature infant at children's hospital
articles.summary: Kieran Ansley allegedly left a premature baby with broken bones and bruises at Helen DeVos Children's Hospital, entering her room 27 times that night.
articles.body: A nurse is accused of beating a prematurely born 4-month-old baby girl at a Michigan hospital, leaving the infant with broken bones and bruises, including injuries to her tongue, according to reports. Kieran Ansley, 43, who was fired from Helen DeVos Children’s Hospital in Grand Rapids, is charged with multiple counts of child abuse. The child was born four months premature but was making progress after spending months in the ICU and was expected to go home in April, WOOD-TV reported. TEXAS DENTIST ACCUSED OF FATAL MISTAKES AFTER 4-YEAR-OLD DIES DURING DENTAL PROCEDURE "She was born at 23 weeks: 1 pound, 1 ounce," her grandfather, Robert Steavens, told WOOD-TV. "And she made it through her due date, ready to go home. And then two days before she was ready to go home, this happened." The girl's mother visited her on April 2. As she approached the room, Ansley "‘jogged’ to cut them off before getting to the room, telling them that the infant had ‘slept through the night,’" court records show. MARYLAND DAD BLAMED 'SATAN' AFTER 2-MONTH-OLD DAUGHTER DIED FROM HORRIFIC HEAD TRAUMA The mother also noticed that the infant's tongue was "blue and black" and that several bruises were on the child that weren't there the night before. Court records show Ansley claimed to have "seen this in the past and it was not a big deal," court records show. During an investigation, one hospital staffer said Ansley "seemed flustered" and "a little bit frustrated" that night. Ansley was also described as being "scatterbrained." OHIO DAYCARE WORKER CONVICTED OF HORRIFIC PHYSICAL ABUSE OF TODDLERS SENTENCED TO YEARS IN PRISON Others recalled Ansley being "heated" and "overwhelmed," court records show. A staff log from the night the infant was allegedly abused showed 32 instances in which someone entered the baby’s room. Ansley accounted for 27 of those visits, the records show, the news station reported. Fox News Digital reached out to Ansley's attorney and the hospital for comment. Defense attorney Damian Nunzio told the news outlet that Ansley has been cooperative during the investigation, spent "many years" working with ICU patients, and is a "very good person." "And we are confident that our investigation will let the truth come to light," Nunzio added. Ansley, who was released on bond and is expected to appear in court on Nov. 10, was fired after the allegations came to light. "We’re trusting in God and healing as a family and trusting the process will move forward."
